newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin still at helm, keeps up busy pace.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin still at helm, keeps up busy pace.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, ordering top officials to work more closely to tackle Russia's problems, has shown he remains firmly in control despite ill health and recent turmoil in his entourage.

Yeltsin, 65, is also keeping up a busy schedule for a man about to undergo heart surgery, with regular talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin set for Tuesday and a meeting scheduled for Thursday with Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma.

On Monday Yeltsin, who suffered two heart attacks last year and is believed to have had a third this summer, impressed communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament, Gennady Seleznyov, with his robust command of events.
"Despite his illness, he is in control of the situation and is taking decisions by himself. I think he is informed on everything going on in the country," Seleznyov told reporters.

Yeltsin, 65, clearly feels relieved after ditching his cantankerous security chief Alexander Lebed, an ambitious ex-soldier accused by political rivals of trying to seize power by stealth during the president's absence from the Kremlin.

In a move designed to prevent future clashes in his government, Yeltsin told Seleznyov he wanted the top four officials from the branches of power to get together regularly to dovetail their decision-making.

"We cannot have people running in different directions and solving questions in their own ways," Yeltsin said in remarks televised from the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow where he is resting ahead of his operation, due in mid-November.

Under Yeltsin's proposal, a new "permanent four" -- Seleznyov, Chernomyrdin, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and Yegor Stroyev, the speaker of the Federation Council upper chamber -- will meet on a regular basis.

"In the current situation such meetings could become an effective mechanism to search for agreed solutions to the most important issues of the country's life," Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters.

Lebed's sudden dismissal after just four months as secretary of the powerful Security Council has ignited fears that a bloody war in breakaway Chechnya might resume. Lebed was the architect of a fragile peace deal that halted 21 months of fighting there.

However Chechen separatist leaders have indicated that they are ready to work with Lebed's successor, moderate former Duma speaker Ivan Rybkin, who also replaces the gruff ex-paratroop commander as Yeltsin's personal envoy to the southern region.
"Rybkin and Lebed are different people but we won't link the results of the peace process with personalities," rebel leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev told Russian television.

Lebed's peace accord is deeply unpopular in the Duma, dominated by hardline communists and nationalists who see it as a humiliating capitulation to the rebels that will trigger the disintegration of the Russian federation.
Another old soldier discarded by Yeltsin bounced back onto the political stage on Sunday, though Alexander Rutskoi insisted he no longer wanted to fight the Kremlin.
Rutskoi, a former vice-president who led a hardline parliamentary rebellion against Yeltsin in 1993 and was briefly jailed, was elected governor of the central Kursk region.
"We do not intend to wage war with the Kremlin or with the authorities," the moustachioed Afghan war veteran said.

"I have said many times that today's Rutskoi is a different Rutskoi. Now I am not interested in the development of the political situation. I am interested in the development of the economy," he told Russian television.
Yeltsin supporters were not impressed by the conciliatory tone of Rutskoi, who will now sit in the Federation Council.
"It's a serious defeat for democracy," said Sergei Belyayev, head of the pro-government Our Home is Russia Duma faction.
Ukraine's Kuchma is expected to raise the issue of Russia's Black Sea Fleet, based in the port of Sevastopol, in his discussions with Yeltsin on Thursday.
Relations between the two ex-Soviet republics have long been dogged by the fleet dispute, which has prevented them from signing a friendship treaty.
In comments bound to upset Kiev ahead of Thursday's meeting, powerful Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov said on Monday that Russia should not concede any ground over the status of Sevastopol.
"Sevastopol is Russian land, it always was and always will be Russian land," Luzhkov, a Yeltsin ally and possible future presidential candidate, told Russian naval veterans in Moscow.
Other Russian politicians, including Lebed, have used the Sevastopol issue to demonstrate their nationalist credentials.
